Fig 1: Distribution of lexical entropy by translation edition. Panels a–f show complete-chapter observations; panels g–l show the arithmetic mean of retained 1,500-regex-word segment entropies within each chapter. Each chapter receives equal weight in the lower panels. HM denotes the Hawkes–Minford edition and YY the Yang–Yang edition. Violin width represents kernel-density estimates, the central line is the median, boxes show the interquartile range, and whiskers extend to observations within 1.5 interquartile ranges. Entropy uses base-2 logarithms. Exact paired tests, adjusted p-values and effect sizes are reported in the corresponding table and supporting data.

Fig 5: Confusion matrices for Random Forest and hard voting on the chapter-grouped held-out set. The same 24 source chapters were selected using random seed 42 at both sampling levels; all observations from those chapters in both editions were excluded from training. Models used all 18 entropy features and were fitted on the remaining 96 chapters. Panels a–b contain 48 chapter observations and panels c–d contain 142 segments. Each cell shows the observation count and percentage within its true-edition row; shading uses row percentages. HM denotes the Hawkes–Minford edition and YY the Yang–Yang edition. Rows represent true editions and columns predicted editions.
Fig 7: SHAP beeswarm plot for the Random Forest model evaluated on 48 held-out chapter observations. Each point is a held-out observation, ordered vertically by mean absolute SHAP contribution. Positive contributions increase the fitted probability of the Yang–Yang edition; negative contributions decrease that probability toward the Hawkes–Minford edition. Color indicates the feature value from low (purple) to high (orange). Tree SHAP used tree-path-dependent perturbation and training path counts stored in the fitted trees. The explained observations were excluded from model fitting. Contributions describe this fitted model and do not identify causal linguistic determinants; correlated entropy predictors can share or redistribute attribution.

Fig 9: Random Forest feature importance calculated as the mean absolute SHAP contribution across the held-out observations shown in Figs 7 and 8. The three largest contributions at each sampling level are highlighted in orange. The rankings describe prediction attribution for each fitted model on its held-out observations. They are not effect sizes, hypothesis-test results, or evidence that the highlighted features causally determine edition differences.
Fig 10: SHAP dependence plots for the three features with the largest mean absolute held-out contribution at each sampling level. Panels a–c show chapter observations and d–f show chapter-matched 1,500-word segments. Each point pairs one observation’s entropy value with its contribution to the fitted Random Forest probability of the Yang–Yang edition; the dashed horizontal line denotes zero contribution. Features were selected from the held-out importance ranking for descriptive presentation. No causal threshold or breakpoint is inferred, and no trend curve is fitted. The same model, split and explanation settings as Figs 7–9 apply.
Fig 4: Five highest-performing individual entropy features at each sampling level. Bars show the highest mean accuracy among the eight prespecified base classifiers under 10-fold sample-stratified cross-validation (shuffle=True, random_state=42). The classifier achieving each displayed value is identified next to the bar. This is an exploratory ranking over classifiers, not a separate held-out estimate. Fold-level variability is supplied in the machine-readable results. Chapter-grouped held-out evaluation is reported separately. LR, logistic regression; NB, Gaussian naive Bayes; K-NN, k-nearest neighbors; SVM, support vector machine; RF, Random Forest; Ridge, ridge classifier; GB, gradient boosting; NN, neural network.
Fig 6: Feature-group classification performance at the chapter and segment levels. Cells report mean accuracy (%) under 10-fold sample-stratified cross-validation (shuffle=True, random_state=42), using the corrected source-chapter extraction. Each row represents six lexical, six syntactic, six n-gram, or all 18 entropy features. Columns represent the eight prespecified base classifiers and the hard-voting ensemble. Colors share a 50–100% scale across panels. These sample-stratified results are descriptive baselines; the chapter-grouped evaluations assess generalization to unseen chapters. Algorithm abbreviations are defined in Fig 4.
